summary: Publishes the information needed to build interoperable applications on the OpenPGP format. It describes the packet formats and methods needed to read, check, generate, and write conforming messages, but does not cover storage or implementation questions. It is a standards-track document, replaced by RFC 9580.

plainLanguage.summary: OpenPGP is the format used by software that encrypts and signs files and email. This RFC describes the bytes: how a message is split into tagged packets, how a signature is laid out, how a random session key encrypts the content, and how the result is turned into printable text for channels that cannot carry raw binary. It gives implementers one agreed-on format so that programs written by different people can read each other's output.

subtitle: The byte-level format of OpenPGP keys, signatures and encrypted messages.

tldr.problem: Independent implementations of PGP-style software had to agree exactly on how keys, signatures and encrypted messages are laid out, so that a message written by one program could be read by another.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a packet format with a tag byte and a length header, a fixed set of packet types, a signature packet with hashed and unhashed subpackets, an integrity-protected encrypted packet, and the ASCII armor text encoding.
tldr.outcome: Two independent implementations can exchange keys and messages without agreeing on anything else. The document was updated by RFC 5581 and later obsoleted by RFC 9580.

facts.label: Packet tag bits
facts.value: 6 in the new format, 4 in the old format

today: RFC 4880 was published in November 2007 as a Proposed Standard. It was updated by RFC 5581, and it has since been obsoleted by RFC 9580, which restates the OpenPGP message format with updated algorithms. It had itself obsoleted RFC 2440 and RFC 1991.

sections.title: What the OpenPGP Format Covers
sections.content:
OpenPGP is the term for security software built on the PGP 5.x code base, formalised first in RFC 2440 and then in this document. The RFC states its scope plainly: it publishes the information needed to build interoperable applications, describing only the format and the methods needed to read, check, generate and write conforming packets that cross a network. It is not a step-by-step guide to writing an application, and it says nothing about how keys or messages are stored.

OpenPGP software combines strong public-key cryptography with symmetric cryptography to provide confidentiality, key management, authentication and digital signatures. The document covers four core technologies: digital signatures, encryption, compression and conversion to radix-64 text.

Because it describes a wire format rather than a protocol with a conversation, the RFC is organised around the pieces of a message: the data elements a message is built from, the packet syntax that wraps them, one section per packet type, the text encoding, and the algorithms that may appear inside. It was a revision of RFC 2440, which itself replaced RFC 1991, the informational description of PGP 2.6.x. The RFC notes that GnuPG is an OpenPGP implementation, and that OpenPGP 2.6.x software used only RSA, MD5 and IDEA for its cryptographic operations.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC describes a file format, not a conversation. It says what bytes make up a key, a signature and an encrypted message, so that two programs written by different people can read each other's files. It leaves out how to store things and how to build an application around them.

sections.title: Encryption with a One-Time Session Key
sections.content:
Confidentiality comes from combining symmetric and public-key encryption. The sender first encrypts the object with a symmetric algorithm, using a session key: a random number generated for that one object and never reused. Because the session key travels with the message, it has to be protected: it is encrypted with the recipient's public key. The full sequence is that the sender creates the message, generates the session key, encrypts the session key with each recipient's public key and puts those encrypted session keys at the start of the message, encrypts the message body with the session key, and the recipient decrypts the session key with their private key and then decrypts the message with it.

A message can instead be protected with a passphrase. The passphrase is turned into a symmetric key by a string-to-key specifier, of which three types are defined: simple, salted, and iterated and salted. The salted forms add eight octets of arbitrary data to the passphrase before hashing, and the iterated form also repeats the hashing a specified number of octets. The RFC recommends salted or iterated-and-salted specifiers, because simple ones are more vulnerable to dictionary attacks, and it deprecates the old PGP 2.x arrangement of a bare cipher identifier with an implicit MD5 hash.

Signing and encryption can be applied to the same message. The order matters: a signature is generated over the message and attached to it, then the message and its signature are encrypted with the session key, and finally the session key is encrypted with the recipient's public key and prefixed to the encrypted block. Implementations should compress the message after applying the signature and before encrypting it.
sections.plainLanguage: OpenPGP does not encrypt a large message with a public key. It makes a fresh random key for that one message, encrypts the message with it, and encrypts that key with the recipient's public key. The recipient unlocks the key with their private key and uses it to read the message. A passphrase can be used in place of the public key, and it is stretched by hashing with salt so that guessing it is slow.

sections.title: Signatures and the Keys They Bind
sections.content:
A digital signature is made in six steps: the sender creates the message, the software hashes it, the software signs the hash with the sender's private key, the binary signature is attached to the message, the receiver keeps a copy of the signature, and the receiver hashes the received message again and checks the hash against the signature. If the check succeeds, the message is accepted as authentic. The RFC notes that the final authority on the validity of a signature rests with the receiver, and that the vagueness of the signature types is a feature rather than a flaw.

Two signature packet versions are defined. Version 3 carries basic signature information, and version 4 is an expandable format built on subpackets. Implementations should accept version 3 and should generate version 4. A version 4 packet holds a version octet, a signature type octet, a public-key algorithm octet, a hash algorithm octet, a hashed subpacket area and an unhashed subpacket area, the left 16 bits of the signed hash value as a quick test, and the signature itself as one or more multiprecision integers. The data being signed and the signature data from the version number through the hashed subpackets are hashed together; the unhashed subpackets are not covered by the signature and should carry advisory information only.

The signature type says what the signature is about: 0x00 for a binary document and 0x01 for a canonical text document, 0x02 for a standalone signature, 0x10 to 0x13 for the four strengths of certification of a User ID, 0x18 and 0x19 for binding a subkey to its primary key, 0x1F for a signature directly on a key, 0x20 and 0x28 for key and subkey revocations, and 0x30 for revoking an earlier certification.

Keys are identified by a Key ID, an eight-octet number. For a version 4 key the fingerprint is the 160-bit SHA-1 hash of a fixed prefix and the whole public-key packet, and the Key ID is the low-order 64 bits of that fingerprint. Two different keys can share a Key ID, though the probability that two different keys share a fingerprint is much smaller. A version 4 key has one primary key, which must be capable of certification, plus any number of subkeys of other types, each tied to the primary key by a binding signature.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is a value made with a private key from a hash of the data. Anyone with the matching public key can recompute the hash and check it, which shows the data has not changed since it was signed. The signature also says what it covers: a file, a name attached to a key, or a revocation. Keys are referred to by a short eight-byte number taken from a hash of the key.

sections.title: Packets, Headers and Tags
sections.content:
An OpenPGP message, keyring or certificate is built from records called packets. Each packet is a chunk of data with a tag that says what the chunk means, and each packet is a header followed by a body. Some packets contain other packets: a compressed data packet, once uncompressed, holds OpenPGP packets.

The first octet of the header is the packet tag. Bit 7 is always one, and bit 6 selects the format: if it is set, the new format is used, where bits 5 to 0 hold the packet tag; if it is clear, the old format is used, where bits 5 to 2 hold the tag and bits 1 to 0 select the length type. Old format packets can only express tags up to 15, so any packet with a tag of 16 or more must use the new format. The RFC recommends the new format unless interoperability with PGP 2.6.x matters.

There are four ways to encode a length in the new format. A one-octet body length covers 0 to 191 octets. A two-octet body length covers 192 to 8383 octets. A five-octet body length covers up to 4,294,967,295 octets. A partial body length is used when the sender does not know the length in advance: it encodes a power of two from 1 to 1,073,741,824 and is followed by that portion of the data and then another length header. Partial body lengths may only be used for literal, compressed or encrypted data packets, the first one must be at least 512 octets long, and the last length header in a packet must not be a partial one.

The packet tags run from 1 to 19 with gaps: 1 is the public-key encrypted session key, 2 the signature, 3 the symmetric-key encrypted session key, 4 the one-pass signature, 5 the secret key, 6 the public key, 7 the secret subkey, 8 the compressed data, 9 the symmetrically encrypted data, 10 the marker, 11 the literal data, 12 the trust packet, 13 the user ID, 14 the public subkey, 17 the user attribute, 18 the symmetrically encrypted and integrity protected data, and 19 the modification detection code. Tags 60 to 63 are private or experimental.
sections.plainLanguage: A message is a list of packets. Each packet starts with a byte that says what kind of packet it is, followed by a length, followed by the data. There are two header styles: an old one that can only name 16 kinds of packet and a newer one that names 64. The length may be written in one, two or five bytes, or in parts when the sender does not yet know how long the data will be.

sections.title: Detecting Tampering With Encrypted Data
sections.content:
Plain encryption does not tell a recipient whether the ciphertext was altered on the way. The Symmetrically Encrypted Integrity Protected Data packet (tag 18) was created for OpenPGP to close that gap. It holds data encrypted with a symmetric algorithm in cipher feedback mode, and the plaintext inside it must end with a Modification Detection Code packet (tag 19). That packet carries a 20-octet SHA-1 hash of the preceding plaintext, including the prefix data and the tag and length octets of the MDC packet itself.

The design deliberately does not use a signature, because many people value the property that a signed message can be denied: the sender cannot prove they wrote it, because anyone could have produced the same signature. The MDC is weaker than a signature but stronger than bare encryption, and the RFC says so in a non-normative note: it is a checksum rather than a message authentication code. Because the hash function is hard-coded to SHA-1 with no parameters, the system cannot be downgraded to a weaker hash; the RFC suggests that the hash may now be worth upgrading.

Any failure of the MDC means the message was modified and must be treated as a security problem, not merely as a data problem. Failures include a difference in the hash values, the absence of an MDC packet, and an MDC packet anywhere but at the end of the plaintext.

The security section adds several warnings. MD5 has been found to have weaknesses and is deprecated: implementations must not generate new signatures with it, though old ones may still be considered valid. The RFC also records the attack published by Jallad, Katz and Schneier in 2002, in which an attacker modifies an encrypted message and gets the user to send the wrongly decrypted text back, which can let the attacker decrypt the message; compressing the data before encryption usually defeats it, because wrongly decrypted data rarely decompresses, and the MDC defeats it as well, provided the user is not allowed to naively return the damaged text. For that reason an implementation should treat a decompression error as a security problem and must treat an MDC failure as one. The section closes with a table of equivalent strengths drawn from NIST Special Publication 800-57, pairing asymmetric key sizes of 1024, 2048, 3072, 7680 and 15360 bits with hash sizes of 160, 224, 256, 384 and 512 bits and symmetric key sizes of 80, 112, 128, 192 and 256 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypted data gives no promise that it arrived unchanged. OpenPGP adds a short hash of the plaintext, computed before encryption and checked after decryption. If the hash does not match, the message was altered, and the program must say so rather than showing the text as if nothing happened. The hash is not a signature, so the sender can still deny having written the message.

sections.title: ASCII Armor for Channels That Carry Text
sections.content:
The native form of an OpenPGP object is a stream of arbitrary octets. Some channels only carry seven-bit printable text, and text that passes through character-set translation or line-ending conversion can be damaged, so OpenPGP defines a printable encoding of the binary data. That encoding is radix-64, and the RFC says implementations should provide it.

Radix-64 has two parts: a base64 encoding of the binary data, identical to the MIME base64 content-transfer-encoding, and a checksum. The checksum is a 24-bit cyclic redundancy check converted to four radix-64 characters and preceded by an equal sign, computed with the generator 0x864CFB and the initialisation 0xB704CE, accumulated over the data before it is encoded rather than over the encoded form. A 24-bit checksum was chosen because it fits evenly into printable base64 and because a non-zero initialisation detects more errors than a zero one.

ASCII armor adds structure around the radix-64 data: an armor header line, any number of armor headers as key-value pairs, a blank line, the encoded data, the checksum, and an armor tail. The header line is the name of the data surrounded by five dashes on each side, and the permitted names are BEGIN PGP MESSAGE for signed, encrypted or compressed files, BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK, BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK, BEGIN PGP MESSAGE, PART X/Y for a message split across parts, BEGIN PGP MESSAGE, PART X for a message split into an unspecified number of parts, and BEGIN PGP SIGNATURE for detached signatures, OpenPGP/MIME signatures and cleartext signatures. Armor headers are not part of the message and are not covered by any signature applied to the message.
sections.plainLanguage: Binary data cannot travel safely through every channel, so OpenPGP can write it as text. The text is base64 with a short checksum at the end, wrapped in lines that begin and end with five dashes, such as a message header or a public key block. The wrapping tells a program what kind of thing it is reading.

fields.name: Bit 6
fields.desc: Set to use the new packet format, clear for the old format.

fields.name: Packet Tag
fields.desc: New format: the tag itself, 0 to 63. Old format: bits 5 to 2, so tags up to 15 only.

viz.caption: THE PACKET TAGS AND WHAT THEY HOLD

items.label: Public-Key Encrypted Session Key
items.desc: Holds the session key, encrypted to one recipient's public key.

items.label: Signature
items.desc: Binds a public key to some data.

items.label: Symmetric-Key Encrypted Session Key
items.desc: Holds a session key protected by a passphrase.

items.label: One-Pass Signature
items.desc: Announces a signature that follows the data.

items.label: Secret-Key
items.desc: The private half of a key.

items.label: Public-Key
items.desc: The public half of a key.

items.label: Secret-Subkey
items.desc: The private half of a subkey.

items.label: Compressed Data
items.desc: Holds one or more packets, compressed.

items.label: Symmetrically Encrypted Data
items.desc: The encrypted body of a message.

items.label: Marker
items.desc: An obsolete literal packet, kept for compatibility.

items.label: Literal Data
items.desc: The data itself, with a file name and a timestamp.

items.label: Trust
items.desc: Trust information supplied by the local keyring.

items.label: User ID
items.desc: A name bound to a key by certification signatures.

items.label: Public-Subkey
items.desc: The public half of a subkey.

items.label: User Attribute
items.desc: Extra attributes of the key holder, such as an image.

items.label: Sym. Encrypted Integrity Protected Data
items.desc: Encrypted data that must end with a modification detection code.

items.label: Modification Detection Code
items.desc: The 20-octet SHA-1 hash of the preceding plaintext.

messages.label: Encrypted session key
messages.note: The one-time session key, encrypted with the recipient's public key. One such packet for each recipient.

messages.label: Encrypted data
messages.note: The message itself, usually compressed and then encrypted with the session key.
